I know redshift is an effect of movement, red moving away and blue coming forward. so it doesn't happen when you're looking at a page or screen, but is it an illusion based on that or just a coincidence of primary colors?
The old 3D glasses being red and blue, is that somehow related to redshift?

The 3D glasses don't have anything to do with redshift. The glasses simply work because two images are projected on top of each other they've tinted one of the images red and the other blue. The glasses make it hard (though not impossible) to see the image meant for the other eye. That is to say that the red lens in the glasses makes the red-tinted image indistinct, so that eye only sees the blue-tinted image. This allows each eye to see a different image and put them together into a 3D image.

Red and blue were chosen because they are on the opposite ends of the color spectrum, so they're the most different two colors. If they'd used colors closer together on the spectrum like blue and green it wouldn't work as well because they wouldn't filter each other out well and you'd still see a doubled blurry image.

Redshift and blueshift are simply changes in your perception of color based on movement. Your eyes gauge color based on the frequency with which light waves hit them. The lower-frequency waves are on the orange to red end of the color spectrum, higher frequency are blue to violet. If you're moving towards an object, you're causing those waves to hit your eye sooner than they normally would, and your eye interprets this as a higher frequency of light, and the object appears to shift in color towards the blue end of the spectrum, thus blueshift.

I get that, but I guess I meant to ask if you think the glasses were inspired by it. It is clear now that it's just a spin on good old fashioned stereoscopy, only incidentally related to the perceived movement towards different ends of the spectrum by starting at different ends of the spectrum.
